questions.subtopic: 3A1 Risk response options. Insurance and the risk
questions.question: A retailer's risk owner buys a cyber insurance policy that covers breach response costs for its online store. Which statement BEST describes how this changes the breach risk?

options.A: The breach risk can now be removed from the risk register
options.B: Part of the financial loss shifts, but likelihood and harm remain
options.C: A breach becomes less likely because the insurer requires controls
options.D: Accountability for harm to customers passes to the insurance company

questions.key_concept: Risk transfer, such as insurance, shifts part of the financial impact; it does not reduce likelihood, harm or accountability.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the policy actually changes: the chance of a breach, the harm it causes, or who pays for it.
questions.correct_explanation: Insurance is a transfer response: it shifts part of the financial consequence to the insurer. It reduces neither the likelihood of a breach nor the harm to customers and operations, and the retailer still answers to customers and regulators. That is why D loses: accountability for the harm cannot be bought. The breach risk stays in the register with its residual rating, and the risk owner keeps monitoring it.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the risk now feels covered. Transferred risk stays in the register with its residual rating, because the breach can still happen and still harm customers.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because insurers sometimes ask for controls. The policy itself does nothing to make a breach less likely; only controls the retailer runs can do that.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the insurer pays the bills. Customers and regulators still hold the retailer accountable for protecting their data, whoever pays the costs.

tips: Eliminate: A and C credit insurance with removing the risk or lowering its likelihood; transfer shifts money only, so the risk stays recorded and just as likely.
Final two: B beats D because transfer moves part of the financial loss, while accountability for the harm stays with the retailer.
Exam cue: when an option says transfer removes the risk or the accountability, treat it as a trap; transfer shifts money, not ownership.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-39 Section 3.3 (Responding to Risk: accept, avoid, mitigate, share or transfer); ISACA Glossary (risk transfer)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 3A1.1 The Four Risk Responses (transfer moves money, not accountability; exam trap 'buying cyber insurance removes the risk'). Public source: NIST SP 800-39 Section 3.3 (risk transfer reduces neither likelihood nor consequences). Original scenario written for KaiSip in our own words; no ISACA Review Manual, QAE, practice-quiz or prep-bank text used. CRISC D3 pilot batch (crisc_d3_001 to 020), 30 Oct 2026.

questions.subtopic: 3A1 Risk response options. Risk within appetite
questions.question: A logistics firm's shipment-tracking risk, owned by the operations director, is now within appetite, but the IT manager proposes an extra monitoring tool. What is the risk analyst's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Buy the tool, because extra monitoring lowers the risk further
options.B: Ask the IT manager to accept the residual risk formally
options.C: Run a cost-benefit analysis of the proposed monitoring tool
options.D: Have the director accept the residual risk and keep monitoring it

questions.key_concept: A risk already within appetite is accepted by its owner and monitored; it does not need further treatment.
questions.pre_read: Find where the risk sits against appetite, and who owns it, before judging the new tool.
questions.correct_explanation: A risk already within appetite needs acceptance and monitoring, not more treatment. The operations director owns the risk, so they accept the residual risk on record and the analyst keeps it under watch. A cost-benefit study weighs treatments that are still needed; here no further treatment is needed, so analyzing the tool spends effort on a question the appetite has already answered.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because more monitoring feels safer. Spending on a risk already within appetite takes budget from risks that are still above it.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the IT manager proposed the tool. The operations director owns this business risk, so acceptance is theirs, not IT's.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because cost-benefit is sound practice. It weighs treatments that are needed; a risk already within appetite needs acceptance and monitoring, not new options.

tips: Eliminate: A adds control to a risk already within appetite, and B gives acceptance to IT instead of the director who owns the risk.
Final two: D beats C because, once risk is within appetite, the response is acceptance and monitoring; cost-benefit work is for treatments that are still needed.
Exam cue: within appetite means accept and monitor; above appetite means treat. Check where the risk sits before weighing any new control.
questions.framework_ref: NIST IR 8286B-upd1 Section 2.3.1 (Risk Acceptance: exposure within risk tolerance is still reported, monitored and managed); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 RA-7 (Risk Response)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 3A1.2 Choosing a Response by Appetite and Cost-Benefit (a risk within appetite needs monitoring, not new spending) and 3A1.3 Residual Risk and Risk Acceptance (the owner accepts). Public source: NIST IR 8286B-upd1 Section 2.3.1. Original scenario written for KaiSip in our own words; no ISACA Review Manual, QAE, practice-quiz or prep-bank text used. CRISC D3 pilot batch (crisc_d3_001 to 020), 30 Oct 2026.

questions.subtopic: 3A1 Risk response options. A service the strategy needs
questions.question: A hospital's telehealth service is central to its growth strategy, and the compliance lead wants it closed because its privacy risk exceeds appetite. What is the BEST recommendation to the risk owner?

options.A: Mitigate with controls until the privacy risk falls within appetite
options.B: Avoid the risk by closing the service until it is secure
options.C: Accept the risk because the service supports the hospital's growth strategy
options.D: Transfer the risk to the platform vendor through the contract

questions.key_concept: Avoidance fits only when an activity is not needed for objectives or no treatment can bring its risk within appetite.
questions.pre_read: Weigh what the business gains from the service against the risk, and notice whether controls could work.
questions.correct_explanation: Avoidance gives up the activity and its benefit, so it fits when the activity is not needed or no response can bring the risk within appetite. Telehealth is central to strategy, and nothing suggests controls cannot work, so the practitioner recommends mitigation down to appetite. Closing the service, even for a time, sacrifices an objective the response is meant to protect. The risk owner then decides.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it removes the exposure at once. It also stops a service central to strategy when controls could bring the risk within appetite.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the service matters. Strategic value does not make a risk above appetite acceptable; it argues for treating the risk, not keeping it as it is.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the vendor runs the platform. Contracts can share costs, but the hospital still answers to patients and regulators for their privacy.

tips: Eliminate: C keeps a risk that exceeds appetite, and D treats a contract as moving the hospital's privacy accountability to the vendor.
Final two: A beats B because avoidance sacrifices an objective the business needs; when controls can bring risk within appetite, mitigation keeps both the service and the limit.
Exam cue: before choosing avoid, ask whether the activity serves a business objective; if it does, look for the response that treats the risk instead.
questions.framework_ref: NIST IR 8286B-upd1 Section 2.3.2 (Risk Avoidance: not conducting the activity when exposure exceeds tolerance); NIST SP 800-39 Section 3.3 (Responding to Risk: accept, avoid, mitigate, share or transfer)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 3A1.1 The Four Risk Responses (avoidance gives up the benefit; exam trap 'avoid any risk that is above appetite'). Public sources: NIST IR 8286B-upd1 Section 2.3.2; NIST SP 800-39 Section 3.3. Original scenario written for KaiSip in our own words; no ISACA Review Manual, QAE, practice-quiz or prep-bank text used. CRISC D3 pilot batch (crisc_d3_001 to 020), 30 Oct 2026.

questions.subtopic: 3A1 Risk response options. Generative AI replies
questions.question: A bank plans to let a generative AI tool draft replies to customers' loan disputes, and the analyzed risk of wrong advice exceeds appetite. Which response should the risk practitioner recommend as BEST?

options.A: Rely on the vendor's contract clause covering losses from wrong replies
options.B: Ban the use of AI tools across the bank until rules exist
options.C: Require a trained staff member to review each draft before sending
options.D: Accept the risk, since staff can correct complaints after replies go out

questions.key_concept: AI risk above appetite is treated with controls such as human review; a vendor clause shifts cost, not accountability.
questions.pre_read: Note where the risk sits against appetite, and whether each option prevents wrong advice or only pays for it.
questions.correct_explanation: The risk exceeds appetite, so it needs treatment. Human review of each draft is a mitigating control aimed at the cause, wrong advice reaching customers, and it keeps the benefit of the tool. A vendor liability clause is a transfer: it may pay back some losses, but customers still receive wrong advice and the bank still answers for it. The risk owner then accepts what remains.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the vendor built the tool. Contract terms share costs; customers still get wrong advice, and regulators hold the bank accountable.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it removes AI risk at once. A bank-wide ban gives up benefits far beyond this use, when a targeted control can bring this risk within appetite.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because errors can be fixed later. The risk is above appetite, and fixing replies after customers act on them does not prevent the harm.

tips: Eliminate: B avoids far more activity than this risk requires, and D keeps a risk above appetite and relies on repairing harm after it happens.
Final two: C beats A because human review stops wrong advice before it reaches customers; a vendor clause shifts part of the cost and none of the accountability.
Exam cue: for AI risk above appetite, look for a control that checks outputs before they take effect, not a contract that pays afterward.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 (AI RMF 1.0) MANAGE 1.3 (responses to high-priority AI risks are developed, planned and documented, including mitigating, transferring, avoiding or accepting); NIST AI 100-1 (AI RMF 1.0) GOVERN 3.2 (roles and responsibilities for human-AI configurations and oversight of AI systems are defined)

Public source: NIST AI RMF 1.0 MANAGE 1.3 and GOVERN 3.2. Original scenario written for KaiSip in our own words; no ISACA Review Manual, QAE, practice-quiz or prep-bank text used. CRISC D3 pilot batch (crisc_d3_001 to 020), 30 Oct 2026.

questions.subtopic: 3A2 Risk and control ownership. Owner for an outage risk
questions.question: A manufacturer's risk register lists the IT department as owner of the risk that a scheduling system outage halts production lines. Whom should the risk practitioner propose as the MOST appropriate risk owner?

options.A: The IT infrastructure manager who runs the scheduling servers
options.B: The enterprise risk committee, acting jointly for the departments
options.C: The production director, whose output targets the outage would hit
options.D: The risk practitioner, who maintains the register and updates its ratings

questions.key_concept: The risk owner is the business manager accountable for the affected objective, with authority to fund and accept the response.
questions.pre_read: Ask who loses if the outage happens, and who controls the budget to respond to it.
questions.correct_explanation: Risk ownership follows accountability for the business outcome and authority to fund and accept the response. The outage threatens production targets, so the production director should own the risk, with IT owning the scheduling controls. The infrastructure manager runs the servers but does not answer for lost output or control the production budget, which is why IT ownership is the trap here.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the system is technical. IT runs the servers as control owner, but the production loss and the decision on the response belong to the business.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the risk touches several areas. Group ownership blurs accountability; one named owner decides, and the others contribute.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the practitioner knows the risk best. The practitioner facilitates and reports but does not own or accept business risk.

tips: Eliminate: B spreads ownership so no one is accountable, and D gives a business risk to the practitioner, who advises but never owns risk.
Final two: C beats A because ownership follows the business objective at stake and the budget to act; IT owns the controls, not the production risk.
Exam cue: ask whose objectives suffer if the risk happens; that manager, not the team running the technology, is the risk owner.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA Glossary (risk owner); NIST IR 8286B-upd1 Section 2.4.3 (Risk Owner: risk escalation and elevation)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 3A2.1 Assigning Risk Owners (ownership follows accountability and budget; exam traps 'IT owns the risk' and joint ownership) and 3A2.2 Control Owners and Validating Ownership. Public source: ISACA Glossary (risk owner). Original scenario written for KaiSip in our own words; no ISACA Review Manual, QAE, practice-quiz or prep-bank text used. CRISC D3 pilot batch (crisc_d3_001 to 020), 30 Oct 2026.

questions.subtopic: 3A3 Vendor/supply chain risk management. Report scope
questions.question: A university relies on its payroll provider's SOC 2 Type 2 report, which excludes the subcontractor that calculates employees' tax deductions. What is the risk analyst's BEST next step?

options.A: Obtain assurance over the subcontractor's tax calculation controls
options.B: Rely on the provider's contract, which makes it liable for any errors
options.C: Accept the report, because Type 2 testing covers a full period
options.D: Recommend ending the contract and bringing payroll back in-house

questions.key_concept: An assurance report covers only its stated scope; a carved-out fourth party needs assurance of its own.
questions.pre_read: Check what the report covers, and which part of the service it leaves out.
questions.correct_explanation: An assurance report covers only the services and parties in its scope. Tax calculation sits with an excluded subcontractor, a fourth party to the university, so the report says nothing about those controls. The analyst should seek assurance over them, such as the subcontractor's own report. A liability clause may recover some costs, but it gives no evidence the deductions are right and leaves employees exposed.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the provider signed up to cover errors. Liability shares cost after the fact; it gives no evidence that deductions are being calculated correctly.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because Type 2 tests operation over time. That testing covers only what is in scope, and the subcontractor was excluded from it.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it would remove the gap. Exit is a large step to take before anyone has assessed the gap or sought the missing assurance.

tips: Eliminate: C trusts a report for a scope it excludes, and D moves to exit the contract before the gap has been assessed.
Final two: A beats B because the risk owner needs evidence the excluded controls work; a liability clause shifts cost but proves nothing about them.
Exam cue: with any assurance report, check its scope and period first; carved-out services and subcontractors need their own assurance.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SR-6 (Supplier Assessments and Reviews); NIST CSF 2.0 GV.SC-07 (supplier and third-party risks are understood, recorded, prioritized, assessed, responded to and monitored over the course of the relationship)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 3A3.2 Ongoing Vendor Monitoring and Assurance Reports (report counts only for its scope; exam trap 'a clean SOC 2 report means the vendor is covered'; fourth parties). Public sources: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SR-6; NIST CSF 2.0 GV.SC-07. Original scenario written for KaiSip in our own words; no ISACA Review Manual, QAE, practice-quiz or prep-bank text used. CRISC D3 pilot batch (crisc_d3_001 to 020), 30 Oct 2026.

questions.subtopic: 3A4 Issues, findings, exceptions and exemptions. Deviation request
questions.question: A clinic's imaging system cannot meet the new encryption standard until next year's vendor upgrade, and its manager asks the risk analyst to approve an exception. What should the analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Approve a one-year exception, since the upgrade date is already set
options.B: Record an exemption that removes the system from the standard
options.C: Require the clinic to stop using the imaging system until it complies
options.D: Assess the risk and propose compensating controls for owner approval

questions.key_concept: An exception is a temporary, owner-approved deviation with compensating controls and an expiry; the practitioner assesses and advises.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether the standard applies to this system, and who may accept the risk of not meeting it.
questions.correct_explanation: The requirement applies but cannot be met for a time, so this is an exception, and granting it means accepting risk, which is the risk owner's decision. The analyst first assesses the risk and proposes compensating controls, such as restricting access to the images, so the owner can approve a time-bound exception. An exemption would wrongly treat the standard as not applying and drop the expiry that forces the upgrade.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the fix date is known. Approving a deviation accepts its risk; that decision belongs to the risk owner, after the risk is assessed.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the system cannot comply now. An exemption excludes a requirement that does not apply; this one applies, so a time-bound exception fits.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it closes the gap. Stopping a clinical system before assessing the risk may harm patient care more than the encryption gap does.

tips: Eliminate: A has the analyst accepting risk by approving the deviation, and C halts a clinical system before its risk has been assessed.
Final two: D beats B because the requirement still applies, so the deviation is a time-bound exception the owner approves; an exemption would remove the deadline to comply.
Exam cue: a temporary gap against a requirement that applies is an exception, with compensating controls, an expiry date and risk-owner approval.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 ID.RA-07 (changes and exceptions are managed, assessed for risk impact, recorded and tracked); ISACA Glossary (compensating control)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 3A4.2 Exceptions and Exemptions (compare table; exam trap 'the risk practitioner can grant a short exception'). Public sources: NIST CSF 2.0 ID.RA-07; ISACA Glossary (compensating control). Original scenario written for KaiSip in our own words; no ISACA Review Manual, QAE, practice-quiz or prep-bank text used. CRISC D3 pilot batch (crisc_d3_001 to 020), 30 Oct 2026.

questions.subtopic: 3B1 Control frameworks, types and standards. Weekly change comparison
questions.question: Each Monday, a hospital's IT team compares last week's firewall changes with approved change tickets and raises an incident for any mismatch. How should the risk practitioner classify this control MOST accurately?

options.A: Preventive, because it stops unapproved changes from taking effect
options.B: Detective, because it finds unapproved changes after they are made
options.C: Corrective, because it restores the firewall to its approved settings
options.D: Deterrent, because staff know their changes will be reviewed weekly

questions.key_concept: A control that reviews events after they happen is detective, even when it targets unauthorized activity.
questions.pre_read: Notice when the comparison happens relative to the change, and what the team does with a mismatch.
questions.correct_explanation: The comparison happens after changes are already live, so the control finds unapproved changes rather than stopping them: it is detective. Calling it preventive overstates protection, because an unapproved rule could be in place for up to a week. Prevention would need approval enforced before a change can be made. Classifying it correctly lets the residual risk rating reflect that week-long exposure.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it targets unapproved changes. It reviews them after they are live, so it cannot stop them from taking effect.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because a mismatch leads to action. The control raises an incident; restoring the settings is a separate corrective step.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because reviews can discourage misconduct. That is a side effect; the control's main function is finding changes that already happened.

tips: Eliminate: C credits the review with restoring settings, which a separate step does, and D names a side effect rather than the control's main function.
Final two: B beats A because the review happens after changes are live; prevention must block a change before it takes effect.
Exam cue: ask when the control acts. Before the event is preventive, after it is detective, and repairing the damage is corrective.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA Glossary (detective control); NIST IR 8286B-upd1 Section 2.3.4 (Risk Mitigation: preventive, deterrent, detective, corrective and compensating controls)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 3B1.1 Control Types by Function (types list; exam trap 'a review of change logs prevents unauthorized changes'). Public sources: ISACA Glossary (detective control); NIST IR 8286B-upd1 Section 2.3.4. Original scenario written for KaiSip in our own words; no ISACA Review Manual, QAE, practice-quiz or prep-bank text used. CRISC D3 pilot batch (crisc_d3_001 to 020), 30 Oct 2026.

questions.subtopic: 3B2 Control design, selection and implementation. Recurring billing errors
questions.question: At a water utility, billing errors keep recurring because staff retype meter readings from handheld devices into the billing system. Which control should the risk practitioner recommend as MOST effective?

options.A: Send readings from the devices into billing automatically
options.B: Have a supervisor review a sample of typed readings daily
options.C: Retrain billing staff on careful data entry every quarter
options.D: Expand the team that corrects bills after customers complain

questions.key_concept: The most effective control addresses the root cause of a risk rather than detecting or correcting its symptoms.
questions.pre_read: Find the step in the process that creates the errors before comparing the controls.
questions.correct_explanation: The root cause is the manual retyping step, so the most effective control removes it: an automated transfer from the devices to billing prevents transcription errors at the source. A supervisor's sample review would catch some errors, but only after they are made and only in the sample, so errors still reach customers. The control owner and risk owner then confirm the cost is proportionate.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because review catches mistakes. It detects some errors after entry, and only in its sample; the retyping that causes them continues.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because people make the errors. Retyping invites mistakes however careful staff are; the process step itself is the cause.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because customers get fixes faster. Correcting bills after complaints limits damage but lets every error reach customers first.

tips: Eliminate: C trains people to work around a flawed step, and D repairs bills only after the error has reached customers.
Final two: A beats B because removing the retyping step fixes the cause; a sample review detects some errors after they are made.
Exam cue: when errors recur from a process step, the BEST control changes or removes that step rather than checking its output.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-39 Section 3.3 Task 3-2 (Evaluation of Alternatives: effectiveness, feasibility and cost); NIST IR 8286B-upd1 Section 2.3.4 (Risk Mitigation: preventive, deterrent, detective, corrective and compensating controls)

questions.subtopic: 3B2 Control design, selection and implementation. Two control options
questions.question: A retailer's card-fraud risk exceeds appetite: control X costs $60,000 a year and brings it within appetite, while control Y costs $250,000 a year and leaves almost none. Which is the risk practitioner's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Control Y, because it leaves the least residual risk
options.B: Both controls together, to reduce fraud as far as possible
options.C: Control X, because it meets appetite at a much lower cost
options.D: Neither control, and accept the fraud risk as it stands now

questions.key_concept: Choose the response that brings residual risk within appetite at a proportionate cost, not the one that removes the most risk.
questions.pre_read: Compare each option's cost with what it achieves against appetite, not just how much risk it removes.
questions.correct_explanation: The goal is residual risk within appetite at a cost proportionate to the benefit. Control X reaches appetite for $60,000; control Y spends $190,000 more each year to push the risk below a level the business has already said it can live with. That money is better spent on risks still above appetite. The risk owner makes the final choice, informed by this comparison.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because less risk sounds better. Below appetite, the extra $190,000 a year buys reduction the business does not need, at the expense of other risks.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because layering feels thorough. Combining both costs even more for reduction beyond appetite, so the cost far exceeds the benefit.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because both options cost money. The risk is above appetite, so keeping it unchanged is not an acceptable response.

tips: Eliminate: B stacks controls past what appetite requires, and D keeps a risk that the stem says exceeds appetite.
Final two: C beats A because, once risk is within appetite, extra spending buys reduction the business has not asked for; proportion decides, not maximum reduction.
Exam cue: when two controls both work, prefer the one that meets appetite at the lower total cost, unless a law or contract requires more.

questions.subtopic: 3B2 Control design, selection and implementation. New review before go-live
questions.question: A risk analyst at a software company is helping the support manager set up a weekly review of bulk customer-data exports. What is MOST important to agree before the review goes live?

options.A: That the analyst performs the first few reviews personally
options.B: That internal audit approves the review design in advance
options.C: A lower residual risk rating to record once reviews begin
options.D: The review's owner, its steps and the evidence each review leaves

questions.key_concept: A new control needs an owner, a documented procedure and an evidence trail, agreed with the control owner before go-live.
questions.pre_read: Separate what the control needs in order to work from what the register will say once it does.
questions.correct_explanation: Before a control goes live, the analyst works with the control owner to agree who runs it, how it is performed and what evidence it leaves. Without these, the review cannot be tested and fails quietly when people change jobs. Recording a lower residual rating is premature: risk counts as reduced only after the review is shown to operate. The risk owner then accepts the new rating.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the analyst knows the risk. Running the control would make the analyst its operator and leave the support team without ownership.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because audit gives assurance. Internal audit assesses controls independently afterward; approving management's design in advance would weaken that independence.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the register should reflect new controls. The rating changes only after the review is shown to work, not when it is planned.

tips: Eliminate: A puts the analyst in the control owner's seat, and B asks internal audit to approve a management control it must later assess independently.
Final two: D beats C because a control needs an owner, a procedure and evidence before it can work; the residual rating changes only after it is shown to operate.
Exam cue: before go-live, look for owner, procedure and evidence; after go-live, look for proof it operates before lowering the risk.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 GV.RR-02 (roles, responsibilities and authorities related to cybersecurity risk management are established, communicated, understood and enforced); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 CA-2 (Control Assessments)

questions.subtopic: 3B3 Control testing methodologies. Evidence for a daily control
questions.question: A bank's control owner says the daily reconciliation of outgoing payment files never misses a day. Which evidence should the risk analyst rely on MOST to confirm the control operates?

options.A: A signed statement from the owner confirming daily completion
options.B: Reconciliation records for a sample of days the analyst selects
options.C: Observation of the owner performing today's reconciliation
options.D: The written procedure that describes each step of the reconciliation

questions.key_concept: For operating effectiveness, evidence across the period that the tester selects beats inquiry and one-time observation.
questions.pre_read: Ask which evidence covers the whole period, and which shows only a single moment or a belief.
questions.correct_explanation: Operating effectiveness needs evidence that the control ran over the period, not just once. Inspecting reconciliation records for days the analyst chooses tests that directly and keeps the selection out of the owner's hands. Watching today's reconciliation shows the control can be done and was done once, while the owner knew they were being observed, so it says little about the other days.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it is formal and signed. It is still inquiry: it records what the owner believes, not evidence that the work was done.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the analyst sees the control first-hand. It covers one day, with the owner aware of being watched, not the whole period.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it shows how the control should work. A procedure supports the design, not whether reconciliations were actually performed.

tips: Eliminate: A is inquiry in written form, and D documents the design rather than showing the control ran.
Final two: B beats C because records for analyst-chosen days cover the period; observation shows one day, while the owner knows they are watched.
Exam cue: for operating effectiveness, prefer evidence across the period that the tester selects, inspects or reperforms over statements or one-time observation.

questions.subtopic: 3C1 Risk action plans. Plan reported complete
questions.question: A telecom's network manager reports that the action plan to require multifactor sign-in for remote access is complete. What should the risk practitioner do FIRST?

options.A: Obtain evidence that multifactor sign-in is now enforced
options.B: Lower the residual risk rating and close the action plan
options.C: Report the completed plan to the risk owner and the risk committee
options.D: Ask internal audit to schedule an audit of remote access

questions.key_concept: The practitioner validates with evidence that an action plan was carried out before re-rating the risk or reporting it complete.
questions.pre_read: Notice who says the plan is complete, and what evidence exists so far.
questions.correct_explanation: A plan reported complete is not yet proven complete. The practitioner first obtains evidence, such as sign-in configuration reports or test results, that multifactor sign-in is enforced for remote users. Only then can the residual risk be re-rated and progress reported. Reporting completion to the owner and committee first would pass on an unverified claim that could lead them to stop watching the risk.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the plan says done. Lowering the rating on the manager's word could understate a risk whose control may not be enforced.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because reporting progress is part of the job. Reporting before validation passes an unverified claim to the people who decide.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because audit is independent. Validating action plans is part of the practitioner's monitoring; waiting for an audit cycle delays a check needed now.

tips: Eliminate: B re-rates the risk on a status report, and D hands a routine validation to internal audit's later cycle.
Final two: A beats C because the practitioner validates completion before reporting it; otherwise the owner and committee decide on an unverified claim.
Exam cue: done is a claim until evidence shows the control is in place and working; validate before you re-rate or report.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 CA-5 (Plan of Action and Milestones); NIST CSF 2.0 ID.RA-06 (risk responses are chosen, prioritized, planned, tracked and communicated)

questions.subtopic: 3C2 Data collection, aggregation, analysis and validation. Mixed rating scales
questions.question: An enterprise risk analyst at a retail group is combining unit risk registers: two units score risks from 1 to 5, and one uses high, medium and low. What should the analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Add each unit's scores together to rank the group's risks
options.B: Average the scores so that each unit carries equal weight
options.C: Map every rating onto one common scale and set of criteria
options.D: List each unit's top risks unchanged in one combined table

questions.key_concept: Risk ratings from different scales must be normalized to common criteria before they are aggregated or compared.
questions.pre_read: Look at how each unit rates its risks before deciding how to combine them.
questions.correct_explanation: Ratings on different scales cannot be compared, added or averaged, so the first step is normalizing them onto the group's common scale and criteria. Only then can duplicates be merged and risks ranked across units. Listing each unit's top risks unchanged keeps them visible, but leaves senior management comparing a 4 with a high and unable to tell which risk matters most.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because totals look decisive. Adding scores from different scales gives numbers with no shared meaning and can bury a severe single risk.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it seems fair to every unit. Averaging still mixes scales and pulls a critical risk toward the middle.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because nothing is lost. Without a common scale, readers cannot compare risks across units or rank them.

tips: Eliminate: A and B do arithmetic on ratings from different scales, which buries severe risks and gives totals with no common meaning.
Final two: C beats D because comparison needs common criteria first; an unchanged list keeps every risk visible but impossible to rank.
Exam cue: before aggregating risk data, normalize it; one scale and one set of criteria come before any ranking, totaling or reporting.
questions.framework_ref: NIST IR 8286C-upd1 Section 2.2 (Normalization of CSRR Information: the same rating criteria enable comparison and tracking); ISACA Glossary (risk aggregation)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 3C2.2 Aggregating and Normalizing Risk Data (normalize before you aggregate; exam trap 'average the units' ratings'). Public sources: NIST IR 8286C-upd1 Section 2.2; ISACA Glossary (risk aggregation). questions.subtopic: 3C3 Risk and control metrics. Indicator for a ransomware risk
questions.question: A hospital's risk analyst is choosing a key risk indicator for the risk of ransomware locking patient records. Which metric is the BEST choice?

options.A: Number of ransomware incidents recorded in the past year
options.B: Number of staff security awareness sessions delivered each quarter
options.C: Average time the help desk takes to reset a password
options.D: Share of servers missing critical patches past their deadline

questions.key_concept: The best key risk indicator is relevant to the scenario and leading: it tracks a driver of the risk, not past incidents.
questions.pre_read: For each metric, ask whether it moves before the event, after it, or not with this risk.
questions.correct_explanation: A good KRI is relevant to the risk scenario, measurable and leading: it moves before the event. Unpatched critical servers are a known driver of ransomware, so a growing share warns that exposure is building while there is still time to act. A count of past incidents is relevant but lagging; it tells the owner the risk has already happened rather than that it is growing.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it measures ransomware directly. Incidents are a lagging outcome; by the time the count goes up, the harm has occurred.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because awareness reduces some attacks. It counts activity delivered, a performance measure, not exposure to this risk.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because help desk metrics are easy to collect. Reset time measures service performance and says nothing about ransomware exposure.

tips: Eliminate: B and C are performance measures of activity and service speed; neither tracks exposure to the ransomware scenario.
Final two: D beats A because a KRI should warn before the event; unpatched servers are a leading driver, while incidents are a lagging outcome.
Exam cue: the BEST KRI is relevant, measurable and leading; prefer a driver of the risk over a count of past losses or incidents.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-55v1 Section 4.4 (Evaluating Methods for Supporting Continuous Improvement: leading and lagging indicators); ISACA Glossary (key risk indicator)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 3C3.1 KRIs, KCIs and KPIs (compare table) and 3C3.2 Selecting Effective KRIs (relevant, measurable, predictive; exam trap 'incident counts make the best early warning'). Public sources: NIST SP 800-55v1 Section 4.4; ISACA Glossary (KRI). Original scenario written for KaiSip in our own words; no ISACA Review Manual, QAE, practice-quiz or prep-bank text used. questions.subtopic: 3C3 Risk and control metrics. Red threshold reached
questions.question: An airline's KRI for unpatched booking servers reaches 12%, above the 8% red threshold agreed with the commercial director, who owns the risk. What should the risk practitioner do FIRST?

options.A: Ask the IT team to patch every affected server immediately
options.B: Report the breach to the commercial director as the risk owner
options.C: Raise the threshold to 15% to reflect current patching levels
options.D: Show the breach in the next quarterly risk report with its trend

questions.key_concept: A KRI threshold breach is escalated to the risk owner, who decides the response; the practitioner does not direct the fix.
questions.pre_read: Note who agreed the threshold and who owns the risk before choosing the first step.
questions.correct_explanation: A threshold breach is escalated to the risk owner, or to the level that set the threshold, through the agreed path, because they decide the response. The commercial director may then direct IT to patch, accept a short delay or fund extra help. Instructing IT directly skips that decision: the practitioner monitors and reports but does not choose or direct the treatment of a business risk.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because patching fixes the cause. Directing the remediation is the owner's call, made with IT; the practitioner's step is escalation.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because current levels may be normal for now. Thresholds follow tolerance, which the risk owner sets, not current performance.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because trends matter. A red breach needs escalation now, not at the next scheduled report.

tips: Eliminate: C moves the limit to fit the breach, and D waits for the reporting cycle when a red threshold calls for prompt escalation.
Final two: B beats A because the owner decides the response to a breach; the practitioner escalates rather than directing IT's work.
Exam cue: when a KRI crosses a threshold, the FIRST move is escalation to the risk owner through the agreed path, not fixing it yourself.
questions.framework_ref: NIST IR 8286B-upd1 Section 2.4.3 (Risk Owner: risk escalation and elevation); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 CA-7(4) (Continuous Monitoring | Risk Monitoring)

questions.subtopic: 3C3 Risk and control metrics. Pricing model indicator
questions.question: An insurer's underwriting team prices home policies with a machine-learning model. Which indicator should the risk practitioner propose as the BEST early warning that the model's risk is growing?

options.A: Weekly shift in input data away from the training baseline
options.B: Number of customer complaints about prices each quarter
options.C: Model accuracy measured once at its last validation
options.D: Percentage of underwriters trained to use the model

questions.key_concept: AI model risk needs leading production indicators, such as input drift, not only lagging signals such as complaints.
questions.pre_read: Ask which indicator would move first if the model began to go wrong.
questions.correct_explanation: Drift in the input data comes before the model's errors show up in prices, so tracking it weekly gives the owner time to retrain or review the model. Complaints are relevant but lagging: they arrive after mispriced policies reach customers, and many affected customers never complain. A single accuracy figure from the last validation cannot show any change in production.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because complaints reflect real harm. They lag behind the errors, arrive quarterly and miss customers who never complain.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because accuracy is the core quality measure. Measured once, it cannot show whether performance has changed since deployment.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because training reduces misuse. It measures an activity, a performance measure, not whether the model itself is degrading.

tips: Eliminate: C is a one-time snapshot that cannot show change in production, and D measures training activity rather than the model's behavior.
Final two: A beats B because input drift moves before pricing errors appear; complaints arrive after customers are harmed.
Exam cue: for AI models, early warning comes from production monitoring of drift and error trends; complaints and incidents confirm harm after it happens.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 (AI RMF 1.0) MEASURE 2.4 (the functionality and behavior of the AI system are monitored when in production); NIST AI 100-1 (AI RMF 1.0) MANAGE 4.1 (post-deployment monitoring plans, including capturing user input, appeal and override)

questions.subtopic: 3C4 Risk and control monitoring techniques. Unread alerts
questions.question: At a law firm, an automated tool emails a shared inbox whenever laptop antivirus is disabled, and the risk analyst finds most alerts unread. What should the analyst recommend as MOST important?

options.A: Add a second monitoring tool to widen coverage of laptops
options.B: Review the shared inbox during the annual internal audit
options.C: Tune the tool so it sends fewer, higher-priority alerts
options.D: Assign each alert type an owner with a required response time

questions.key_concept: Automated monitoring reduces risk only when each alert has an owner who responds within a set time.
questions.pre_read: Ask what happens after an alert is sent, and who is expected to act on it.
questions.correct_explanation: Monitoring reduces risk only when someone acts on what it finds. Alerts sent to a shared inbox have no owner, so disabled antivirus goes unanswered. Giving each alert type a named owner and a response time, with tracking to closure, turns detection into response. Tuning down the noise helps, but fewer alerts in an unowned inbox would still go unread.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because broader coverage sounds safer. More alerts into an unowned inbox add volume without adding any response.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because audit gives independent review. A yearly look leaves disabled antivirus unanswered for months; these alerts need same-day handling.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because alert fatigue is real. Tuning reduces noise, but someone still has to own and act on the alerts that remain.

tips: Eliminate: A adds more alerts to a queue nobody works, and B checks on an audit cycle a risk that needs same-day response.
Final two: D beats C because tuning reduces noise, but without an owner and a response time even important alerts go unanswered.
Exam cue: when monitoring exists but nothing happens, the fix is ownership and response, not more or different monitoring.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-137 Section 3.5 (Respond to Findings); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 CA-7 (Continuous Monitoring)

questions.subtopic: 3C5 Risk and control reporting techniques. Board committee report
questions.question: A regional bank's risk manager is preparing the quarterly IT risk report for the board risk committee. Which content is MOST appropriate for this audience?

options.A: Every open vulnerability, listed by system and severity
options.B: A heat map of every registered risk at its current rating
options.C: Risks beyond appetite, their trend and decisions needed
options.D: Results of each control test performed during the quarter

questions.key_concept: Board risk reporting shows the profile against appetite, trends and the decisions needed, not operational detail.
questions.pre_read: Think about which decisions the board makes, then pick the content that supports them.
questions.correct_explanation: The board sets appetite and makes the major risk decisions, so its report should show where the profile sits against appetite, which way key risks are moving and what it is being asked to decide. A heat map of every risk shows position but not trend or the request, and buries the few risks that need board attention among many that do not.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because full detail looks transparent. Vulnerability lists suit the teams who fix them; the board cannot act on them directly.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because heat maps are a familiar board format. Without trend or a decision request, it shows where risks sit, not what the board must do.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because control results show assurance. Test-by-test detail suits risk and control owners; the board needs the overall effect against appetite.

tips: Eliminate: A and D give the board operational detail that suits the teams and owners who act on it, not the body that sets appetite.
Final two: C beats B because the board needs risks against appetite, their trend and the decision asked of it; a full heat map shows position only.
Exam cue: match the report to its reader's decisions; the board gets the profile against appetite and clear asks, owners get their risks and actions.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-137 Section 3.4 (Analyze Data and Report Findings: recipients, content, format and frequency of reports); NIST CSF 2.0 GV.OV-01 (cybersecurity risk management strategy outcomes are reviewed to inform and adjust strategy and direction)

questions.subtopic: 3C6 Monitoring and reporting of emerging risks. Rules under consultation
questions.question: A pharmacy chain is piloting an AI tool for patient reminder messages when the risk analyst learns that regulators are consulting on rules for AI in patient communications. What should the analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Pause the AI pilot until the final rules are published
options.B: Record an emerging risk with its uncertainty and an owner
options.C: Wait for the final rules before assessing any possible impact
options.D: Rate the regulatory risk as critical to secure budget quickly

questions.key_concept: Emerging risks are recorded early with stated uncertainty, an owner and a review date, then refined as evidence grows.
questions.pre_read: Notice how certain the new rules are, and what each option does with that uncertainty.
questions.correct_explanation: A consultation is an early signal: the rules may change the pilot's obligations, but their content and timing are uncertain. The analyst records it as an emerging risk, with its uncertainty stated, a business owner and a short review date, then refines it as the rules take shape. Pausing the pilot now gives up its benefit on a guess about rules that do not yet exist.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it avoids breaking future rules. It gives up the pilot's benefit before anyone knows what the rules will require.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the rules are not final. Waiting leaves no time to prepare; emerging risks are recorded early and refined as they develop.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it gets attention. Overstating certainty misdirects budget and damages trust; the rating should reflect what is actually known.

tips: Eliminate: C waits until the rules are final, leaving no time to prepare, and D overstates a risk whose details are still unknown.
Final two: B beats A because the rules are still uncertain; recording and owning the risk keeps the pilot's benefit while preparing for whatever the rules require.
Exam cue: for an emerging risk, record it early with its uncertainty, an owner and a review date; neither dismiss it nor treat it as certain.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 (AI RMF 1.0) GOVERN 1.1 (legal and regulatory requirements involving AI are understood, managed and documented); NIST SP 800-39 Section 3.4 (Monitoring Risk: compliance, response effectiveness and risk-impacting changes)
